title: BIP-39 — the standard behind your 12/24 words
plain: Your Bitcoin wallet — the app or device that guards your money — is built from a very long random number. Nobody can memorize that, so wallets turn it into a short list of simple words, usually 12 or 24. BIP-39 is the rulebook for how. 'BIP' means Bitcoin Improvement Proposal — a numbered design that wallet makers agree to follow. Because everyone follows the same rulebook, words created by one wallet can be restored in another. Here is how the words are made. First, the wallet creates entropy, which just means fresh randomness — like thousands of coin flips nobody can predict or repeat. BIP-39 allows 128 to 256 bits of it. A bit is one yes-or-no choice, so more bits means a harder puzzle for a thief. Next, the wallet calculates a checksum — a small fingerprint taken from the randomness — and sticks it on the end. Software uses the checksum to notice most typing mistakes. The combined bits are chopped into chunks of 11 bits, and each chunk becomes a number from 0 to 2047 that points to one word on a fixed list of 2048 words (the wordlist). The list avoids confusing pairs like 'build' and 'built'. 128 bits gives 12 words; 256 bits gives 24. The words are not a password you invent. They are randomness written in human-friendly form, easy to put on paper. Never pick your own words: phrases people choose are predictable, and BIP-39 was never meant for that. When you use the words, software runs them through a fixed formula and always gets the same seed — a 512-bit number the wallet builds all of its private keys from. Private keys are the secret numbers that let you spend. An optional passphrase — an extra secret password on top of the words — creates a completely different wallet; forget it and its money is unreachable. Never translate your words into another language: that also makes a different wallet. Finally, the checksum is small, so it catches most typing errors, not all — check every word when you copy them.
technical: BIP-39, 'Mnemonic code for generating deterministic keys' (assigned 2013-09-10; status: Deployed; MIT license; authors Palatinus, Rusnak, Voisine, Bowe), specifies how entropy becomes a mnemonic sentence and how the sentence becomes a binary seed. Generation: create ENT bits of entropy, where ENT is a multiple of 32 within 128-256 bits (128, 160, 192, 224, or 256). Compute CS = first ENT/32 bits of SHA-256(entropy); append to entropy; split the ENT+CS bits into 11-bit groups, each an index 0-2047 into a 2048-word wordlist. MS = (ENT+CS)/11, yielding 12, 15, 18, 21, or 24 words. Wordlists are sorted (binary search/trie friendly), avoid similar pairs such as build/built, are uniquely identified by each word's first four letters, and are UTF-8 NFKD encoded. Seed derivation: PBKDF2 with HMAC-SHA512 as the pseudo-random function, 2048 iterations, 512-bit output; password = mnemonic sentence (UTF-8 NFKD); salt = 'mnemonic' + passphrase (UTF-8 NFKD), empty string if no passphrase. The seed feeds BIP-32 or similar deterministic wallets. Sentence-to-seed conversion is independent of sentence generation; software must checksum-validate mnemonics not generated by the algorithm and warn on failure. Shortcomings per the BIP: the seed depends on the wordlist, so translating a mnemonic to another wordlist yields a completely different seed; the conversion is one-way (an arbitrary BIP-32 seed cannot be represented as a sentence); the checksum is short (source: 1-in-256 random errors missed, no error correction); there is no versioning scheme (largely mitigated by BIP-380 descriptor wallets). Non-English wordlists are strongly discouraged since most wallets support only English. Every passphrase produces a valid seed (plausible deniability). SLIP-0039 is the authors' proposed successor. Test vectors use passphrase 'TREZOR' (github.com/trezor/python-mnemonic, vectors.json).

claims.claim: BIP-39 is a deployed specification, assigned 2013-09-10 under the MIT license, describing a mnemonic code for generating deterministic wallets.
claims.source: BIP header block (Title, Status, Assigned, License).

claims.claim: A BIP-39 mnemonic must encode entropy in a multiple of 32 bits, with the initial entropy length (ENT) allowed to be 128-256 bits.
The checksum is the first ENT/32 bits of the SHA-256 hash of the initial entropy and is appended to the end of the entropy.
The concatenated entropy-plus-checksum bits are split into groups of 11 bits, each encoding a number from 0-2047 that serves as an index into a wordlist.
CS = ENT/32 and MS = (ENT+CS)/11, giving word counts of 12, 15, 18, 21, and 24 for ENT values of 128, 160, 192, 224, and 256 bits respectively.
claims.source: Table in Generating the mnemonic section.

claims.claim: An ideal wordlist is designed so the first four letters unambiguously identify each word, avoids similar word pairs like build/built, is sorted for efficient lookup, and is encoded in UTF-8 using NFKD normalization.
claims.source: Wordlist section, criteria a, b, and c.

claims.claim: If no passphrase is present, an empty string is used instead.

The binary seed is derived with PBKDF2 using HMAC-SHA512 as the pseudo-random function, 2048 iterations, and a 512-bit output; the password is the mnemonic sentence (UTF-8 NFKD) and the salt is 'mnemonic' + passphrase (UTF-8 NFKD).
The derived seed can be used to generate deterministic wallets using BIP-0032 or similar methods.
claims.source: Abstract and From mnemonic to seed section.

claims.claim: Every passphrase generates a valid seed, providing plausible deniability; only the correct passphrase makes the desired wallet available.
BIP-39 is not intended as a way to process user-created sentences (brainwallets) into a wallet seed.
Since the vast majority of BIP-39 wallets support only the English wordlist, using non-English wordlists for generating mnemonic sentences is strongly discouraged.
Because seed derivation uses the mnemonic sentence directly rather than the original entropy, translating a mnemonic to a different wordlist creates a completely different seed.
The conversion from BIP-39 sentence to BIP-32 seed is one-way only; an arbitrary BIP-32 seed cannot be represented as a BIP-39 sentence.
The checksum is short: per the source, 1-in-256 random errors will be missed, and it cannot assist in correcting errors.
claims.source: Shortcomings section (flagged for review — see notes).

claims.claim: BIP-39 has no versioning scheme; this is now largely mitigated by use of descriptor wallets (BIP-0380) in addition to a seed.
The authors of BIP-39 proposed SLIP-0039 as an intended successor improving on the identified shortcomings.

The test vectors use the passphrase 'TREZOR' and are published at github.com/trezor/python-mnemonic (vectors.json), with additional Japanese wordlist tests at github.com/bip32JP/bip32JP.github.io (test_JP_BIP39.json).

warnings: Never share your 12/24 words with anyone — anyone who has them can take the Bitcoin.
Never make up your own word sentence or choose the words yourself; phrases people invent are predictable and can be guessed by attackers.
Adding a passphrase creates a completely different wallet — if you forget the passphrase, the funds in that wallet cannot be recovered.
Never translate your seed words into another language or wordlist — the translation produces a different wallet and your funds will appear missing.

notes_for_reviewer: 1) Checksum-miss figure: the source states '1-in-256 errors will be missed', which matches the 24-word case (8-bit checksum); for 12-word seeds the checksum is only 4 bits, so a random single-word error would pass roughly 1-in-16 times — consider clarifying per word count. 2) Risk class judgment call: chose 'caution' because the source is a specification rather than a step-by-step destructive procedure, but the passphrase trap (each passphrase = different wallet; forgotten = funds unreachable) and the translation trap are severe for inheritors and could justify 'danger'. 3) Level judgment call: tagged intermediate because of the construction and derivation mechanics; a simpler novice companion entry ('What are seed words?') may be warranted. 4) Staleness: the claim that the vast majority of BIP-39 wallets support only the English wordlist reflects the source text and should be re-verified against the current wallet ecosystem. 5) The plain-text statement that words from one wallet can be restored in another is an inference from BIP-39 being a shared standard, not a verbatim source claim. 6) Source was provided as a local cache file; I cited the canonical GitHub BIPs URL — confirm this matches citation policy. 7) SLIP-0039 is called an 'intended successor' by the authors, but adoption is limited; the entry does not advise switching to it.
